analytic.title: Mutex Scheduling Mechanism Analysis and Performance Evaluation under the RT-Thread Open Source Framework

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: A mutex is an important synchronization tool in real-time operating systems (RTOS) used to protect shared resources, ensuring that at any given moment only one thread can access the resource. This prevents race conditions and data conflicts. This paper provides an in-depth analysis of the application scenarios, workflow, and scheduling timing of mutexes in RT-Thread, offering insights and reference points for designing new RTOSs.Using the RT-Thread on the ARM Cortex-M series STM32L431 microcontroller as an example, we designed three threads of equal priority (red light, blue light, green light) to demonstrate how threads request, acquire, use, and release mutexes. This design verifies that using mutexes ensures that threads access shared resources in a sequential and mutually exclusive manner, thereby avoiding issues such as data inconsistency and deadlocks.Furthermore, this paper adopts a process analysis method based on printf output, innovatively utilizing global variables to store timestamps combined with the SysTick timer for time calculation. This approach not only analyzes the response times for locking and unlocking mutexes but also examines the distribution of time during which threads hold the mutex. By effectively reducing the error introduced by the printf function, this method enhances the accuracy of experimental results, providing a new perspective for comprehensively evaluating the performance of mutex scheduling mechanisms.

div.head: INTRODUCTION
div.p: RT-Thread Real-Time Operating System (RTOS) is a domestically developed open-source RTOS. It is characterized by high reliability, ultra-low power consumption, and a rich set of easy-to-use middleware components. RT-Thread is one of the most widely adopted Internet of Things (IoT) operating systems among developers in the fields of embedded artificial intelligence and IoT [1] . Mutexes serve as one of the synchronization and communication mechanisms between tasks or between tasks and interrupts within an RTOS. They are primarily used to ensure exclusive access to shared resources. Analyzing and studying their scheduling mechanisms can aid in understanding how an RTOS operates and significantly assist in the design of new RTOSs [2] .Currently, several scholars have conducted research on mutex mechanisms. Wang Tingchen designed a software example that uses mutexes to protect public resources, allowing for an understanding of mbedOS's scheduling mechanism through observing changes in light and serial port output information [3] . Zhang Linyan pointed out that in operating systems, mutexes can coordinate resource access among multiple tasks, serving as a common task synchronization method. The correctness of their functionality is crucial for ensuring the accuracy of multitasking applications [4] . Ye Keyang noted that operating systems address priority inversion issues using the priority inheritance protocol. Overall, they employ mutex semaphores, arranging waiting threads either by priority or in a first-in-first-out queue to lock these semaphores, thereby avoiding priority inversion phenomena [5] . Ma Yunnan highlighted that in the MiniCore real-time operating system, mutexes are used to control task permissions for accessing critical resources, ensuring safe access to such resources and preventing priority inversion and deadlocks due to improper use of critical resources [6] .

div.head: II. DEFINITION AND APPLICATION SCENARIOS OF MUTEX
div.p: A. Mutex A mutex, short for mutual exclusion (also referred to as a mutex lock), is one of the fundamental synchronization primitives used to protect critical sections (or shared resources) in an operating system. It ensures that only one thread can operate on the critical section at any given time, thereby achieving synchronization between threads. Mutex operations consist solely of locking and unlocking, with each thread capable of performing these actions on a mutex. Operations must follow the order of locking before unlocking. Once a thread locks a mutex, no other thread can lock it until the original thread has performed an unlock operation. This behavior represents exclusive access to a resource. In environments without an operating system, exclusive access to resources is typically achieved by declaring independent global variables and using conditional statements within the main loop to check specific values of those global variables.

div.head: B. Scenarios of Mutex Application
div.p: In a computer system, there are many constrained resources, such as hardware resources like serial communication interfaces, card readers, and printers, as well as software resources such as shared global variables, queues, and data. Taking the use of serial communication as an example, suppose there are two threads: Thread A outputs "Thread A" from the serial port, and Thread B outputs "Thread B" from the serial port. Execution starts with Thread A, and both Thread A and Thread B have the same priority.Without using a mutex, due to the operating system's time-slice rotation mechanism, Task A and Task B would execute alternately. If Thread A hasn't finished sending content to the serial port and Thread B starts sending its content, it would lead to jumbled output, resulting in incorrect outcomes. After the process, the serial port might output "ThreadThreadAB", which is far from the expected output of "Thread A" and "Thread B".When using a mutex, after Thread A acquires the serial port, Thread B must wait until Thread A completes its transmission and releases the serial port before Thread B can acquire the serial port to send its data. Through this "queuing" process, the serial port can correctly output "Thread A" followed by "Thread B", ensuring the correctness of the program.

div.head: III. THEORETICAL ANALYSIS OF MUTEX SCHEDULING MECHANISM BASED ON THE RT-THREAD OPEN-SOURCE FRAMEWORK
div.p: A. Creating a Mutex Before using a mutex, it is necessary to call the function for creating a mutex variable to generate a pointer variable to a mutex structure. The process of creating a mutex involves several steps: First, allocate a mutex object; second, initialize the mutex kernel object, setting up a doubly linked list to record threads that are blocked while attempting to access this mutex; then, initialize the mutex's value to 1, set the thread holding the mutex to RT_NULL, the default priority of the thread holding the mutex to 0xFF, and the number of times the thread holds the mutex to 0.

Finally, configure the blocking wake-up mode of the mutex. Objects created with the RT_IPC_FLAG_PRIO flag will, when multiple threads are waiting for a resource, grant the resource to the thread with the higher priority first. In contrast, objects created with the RT_IPC_FLAG_FIFO flag will grant the resource to waiting threads in the order they arrived.

div.head: B. Acquiring a Mutex
div.p: The function to acquire a mutex is called with a specified waiting time during which the designated mutex is attempted to be obtained. The process of acquiring a mutex involves the following steps:It checks whether the thread attempting to acquire the mutex is the same as the one that currently holds it. If they are the same, the ownership count of the mutex is incremented by 1, and the thread does not get suspended.If they are not the same, it then checks if the mutex is locked. If it is not locked, the current thread successfully acquires the mutex, sets the original priority and the ownership count for the mutex holder, and locks the mutex.If the mutex is already locked, it checks whether the acquiring thread should wait. If the wait time equals 0, an error indicating timeout is returned.Otherwise, the current running thread is inserted into the mutex's blocked list. If the priority of the thread attempting to acquire the mutex is higher than that of the thread holding the mutex, the priority of the mutex holder is elevated to match that of the acquiring thread (priority inheritance).If the wait time is greater than 0, the thread's wait time must be set, and a timer is started to place the current thread in a delay list. Meanwhile, the highestpriority thread is selected from the ready list to prepare for execution.The flow for executing the acquisition of a mutex is illustrated in Figure 1.

div.head: C. Releasing a Mutex
div.p: The function to release a mutex is called to unlock the specified mutex. The process of releasing a mutex involves the following steps:It checks whether the current thread is the same as the thread that holds the mutex, ensuring only the thread holding the mutex can release it.If they are the same thread, the ownership count for the mutex holder is decremented by 1.If the ownership count of the mutex holder equals 0, it then checks if the thread's original priority needs to be restored and examines the mutex's blocked list for any threads waiting on the current mutex.If there are waiting threads in the blocked list, the first thread in the list is awakened and removed from both the blocked list and the delay list. The new holder thread, its priority, and the holder count are set accordingly.If there are no waiting threads, the mutex is unlocked, and the owner information is cleared, restoring the default priority.Finally, it checks if a thread rescheduling is necessary.The flow for executing the release of a mutex is illustrated in Figure 2.

div.head: IV. MUTEX-BASED SCHEDULING PRACTICE FOR THREADS WITH EQUAL PRIORITY
A. Analysis of Mutex Scheduling Timing
div.p: To clarify the method of using a mutex and how threads perform exclusive access to resources, a timing analysis of the scheduling of threads with equal priority based on mutexes is conducted. In this analysis, vertical rectangular blocks represent the effective running time of threads or lists; solid arrows indicate thread execution, entering a list, or applying for a mutex; and dashed arrows represent fetching a thread (or mutex) from a list or returning the result of a mutex application. The analysis of scheduling for threads with equal priority based on mutexes is illustrated in Figure 3.

div.head: Red
B. Segmental Analysis of the Mutex Scheduling Process
div.p: This experiment segments the process of using a mutex and provides the execution results for each segment, allowing users to experience how mutexes can be used to achieve exclusive access to resources by threads. The small lights change their brightness state in the sequence of red light, blue light, and green light, ensuring that at any given moment, only one light is on, preventing any mixed colors. Due to the threads having the same priority, the SysTick interrupt occurs every 1 ms, and round-robin scheduling of threads happens every time slice (10 ms).

div.head: 1) Thread Initialization
div.p: In the test project, upon power-on of the chip and during the startup sequence, the process eventually transitions to the main thread function app_init for execution. Within this function, three user threads for the red light, blue light, and green light are created along with a mutex object named g_single_light_mutex. The red light, blue light, and green light threads are then initiated in sequence, followed by the termination of the app_init function. Afterward, RT-Thread takes over to manage the scheduling and execution of the threads.

The Red Light Thread Requests to Lock the Mutex After terminating the main thread, RT-Thread retrieves the highest-priority thread from the ready list (which is now the Red Light Thread) and activates it for execution. The Red Light Thread requests to lock the mutex, triggering a PendSV interrupt. The mutex is successfully locked because the mutex lock value is 0, indicating that the Red Light Thread's request to lock the mutex succeeds. Upon successful locking, the mutex lock value changes to 1, and the request returns as successful. The red light is then toggled on or off synchronously.

div.head: ) The Blue Light Thread Requests to Lock the Mutex
div.p: The Blue Light Thread attempts to lock the mutex and triggers a PendSV interrupt. Since the mutex is already locked by the Red Light Thread (the mutex lock is set to 1), the Blue Light Thread fails to acquire the mutex. The Blue Light Thread is then placed into the mutex blocked list, and the Green Light Thread is retrieved from the ready list to prepare for execution.

div.head: 4) The Green Light Thread Requests to Lock the Mutex
div.p: The Green Light Thread requests to lock the mutex, which triggers a PendSV interrupt. Since the mutex is already locked by the Red Light Thread (mutex lock is 1), the Green Light Thread's request to acquire the mutex fails. The Green Light Thread is then placed into the mutex blocked list, and the Red Light Thread is retrieved from the ready list to prepare for execution.

The Red Light Thread Unlocks the Mutex The Red Light Thread requests to unlock the mutex. Since the mutex was locked by the Red Light Thread, it successfully unlocks the mutex, and after unlocking, the mutex lock becomes 0. At this point, the mutex is released and transferred to the Blue Light Thread, which is waiting for the mutex. Afterward, the Red Light Thread begins a new cycle of requesting to lock the mutex. The Blue Light Thread is placed into the ready list and becomes the owner of the mutex, indicating that the Blue Light Thread has successfully locked the mutex, and the mutex lock becomes 1. The system returns a successful unlock of the mutex and toggles the state of the blue light (turns it on or off).

Next, the Blue Light Thread and Green Light Thread unlock the mutex in a process similar to that of the Red Light Thread, with comparable steps and output results; therefore, it will not be reiterated here.

div.head: C. Experimental Conclusion
div.p: During the experiment, the Red Light Thread successfully called the rt_mutex_take function to lock the single-color light mutex, setting the mutex lock to 1. The Red Light Thread then toggled the red light on or off. At this point, any request to access the red light was denied. When the Red Light Thread locked the single-color light mutex, both the Blue Light Thread and the Green Light Thread failed in their attempts to lock the same mutex and were placed into the mutex blocked list. They remained there until the Red Light Thread unlocked the single-color light mutex, after which they were removed from the blocked list and obtained the single-color mutex, allowing them to toggle their respective lights.Since the single-color light mutex was locked by the Red Light Thread, it was able to successfully unlock it. the Red Light Thread unlocked the single-color light mutex, setting the mutex lock back to 0 and entering a waiting state. At this moment, the singlecolor light mutex was transferred from the mutex list to the Blue Light Thread, which had been waiting for the singlecolor light mutex. The Blue Light Thread became the owner of the single-color light mutex, indicating that it successfully locked the single-color light mutex, with the mutex lock set to 1, and it toggled the blue light on or off. he Blue Light Thread unlocked the single-color light mutex, setting the mutex lock back to 0. The Green Light Thread, which was still in a waiting state, then became the owner of the single-color light mutex. the Green Light Thread unlocked the single-color light mutex, and the Red Light Thread relocked the single-color light mutex, thereby completing one cycle of this process.

div.head: V. PRINTF DEBUGGING METHOD
A. Analysis Using the printf Function
div.p: In RT-Thread, the real-time analysis of mutex scheduling is primarily achieved through the use of the printf function. In the embedded systems domain, the printf function is commonly used for breakpoint debugging to locate bugs by outputting effective prompt information that aids in understanding the dynamic execution process of a program [7] . However, one issue with printf is its relatively slow output speed, which can significantly impact the system's real-time performance when directly used for timing analysis [8] . In this case study, under a core clock frequency of 48 MHz, outputting a single character takes an average of approximately 80 μ s, indicating that the operation of outputting characters consumes a considerable amount of time.This delay might not be noticeable during coarse timing analysis with longer periods but can have severe consequences in RT-Thread, where even second-, millisecond-, or microsecond-level errors could lead to significant issues due to its high real-time requirements. Therefore, when using printf for precise real-time analysis, it is essential to employ subjective programming techniques to mitigate this timing error.

div.head: B. Usage of the printf Function
div.p: During testing, the actual execution time of a code segment is typically determined by calculating the time difference between the start and end points of the code. To avoid significant timing errors introduced by directly adding printf statements at both ends of the test code, one can use global variables to store the start and end times. The printf outputs are then performed outside the test code. Assigning values to global variables occurs on the nanosecond level, which can be disregarded as it has negligible impact. This approach ensures more accurate results.In RT-Thread, there exists a SysTick timer that uses clock tick interrupts for overall task scheduling. This timer is a 24-bit decrementing counter with a default interrupt period of 1 ms, corresponding to 48,000 counts in the SysTick counter. Each tick interrupt increments the kernel tick count variable osRtxInfo.kernel.tick within the RT-Thread kernel to record the number of ticks. Therefore, based on the tick count and the SysTick counter value, the current time can be effectively calculated, with the time unit being milliseconds (ms). The specific calculation process based on the SysTick timer is shown in Table 1.

div.head: VI. SCHEDULING PERFORMANCE ANALYSIS
A. Instruction Cycle
div.p: In embedded systems, the clock cycle, also known as the oscillation cycle, refers to the system's main frequency. The machine cycle is the time required to complete a basic operation, such as fetching an instruction, reading from or writing to memory, which is typically the shortest time needed to read an instruction from memory. The instruction cycle refers to the time required to execute a single instruction, composed of multiple machine cycles. Different instructions require different numbers of machine cycles. For ARM Cortex-M series microcontrollers, the instruction cycle for executing assembly language operations is usually one cycle, but specific instructions or operational conditions can lead to an increase in the number of cycles.

div.head: B. Analysis of Theoretical Response Time for Locking Delay
div.p: The theoretical time required for threads to lock and unlock a mutex is a critical performance metric for evaluating the real-time performance of RT-Thread's mutex synchronization mechanism. Real-time performance software testing involves measuring the execution time between any two points in the kernel code by reading the system clock through system calls. This forms an essential part of designing and assessing the performance of a realtime embedded system [9] .In this engineering framework, based on the RT-Thread platform and using the ARM Cortex-M series STM32L431 microcontroller, the PendSV interrupt triggers the mutex operations. By comparing the theoretical time with the actual execution time for thread requests to lock the mutex, we can analyze the scheduling timing from the start of the serial interrupt call requesting the mutex lock until the successful locking of the mutex.According to the compiled .lst file, the process corresponding to this sequence involves 617 machine instructions. With a system clock frequency of 48 MHz for the test chip, each machine instruction takes approximately1/48μs (i.e., one instruction cycle takes 0.0208μs). Therefore, the theoretical execution time, or response time, for this process is approximately 12.8336μs. Each machine instruction's execution time is benchmarked against the time it takes to execute a single no-operation instruction.Key functions involved in the mutex locking process, along with their corresponding machine code and assembly instructions, are summarized in Table 3. Due to space limitations, only the first and last two machine codes are listed for sequences longer than ten instructions, with ellipses indicating the omitted middle instructions.

div.head: C. Analysis of Actual Response Time for Locking Delay
div.p: The actual response time can vary based on hardware factors but generally does not deviate significantly from the theoretical response time. The actual response time of PendSV scheduling can be effectively measured using the SysTick clock within the system.In the test project, we first define two global variables in the include.h header file: G_VAR_PREFIX vuint32_t a and G_VAR_PREFIX vuint32_t b. In the thread_redlight.c file, before the mutex acquisition statement rt_mutex_take(g_single_light_mutex, RT_WAITING_FOREVER), we insert the time assignment statement a = rt_tick_get();and after it, we insert another time assignment statement b = rt_tick_get();By recording the SysTick counter value (Val) and the number of SysTick interrupts (Num), we can then calculate the actual time elapsed. Therefore, the count value for the period during which the mutex is locked,ΔV=(Numend-Numstart)×48000+(Valstart-Valend), can be used to calculate the time duration ΔT=tend-tstart=ΔV/48μs. In the red light thread, blue light thread, and green light thread, printf is used to output the two time values and their corresponding differences. We conducted a test with one hundred iterations, removing results where the rt_tick values differed to exclude anomalous data. After filtering out these discrepancies, the resulting time differences were consistently 10.8μs, indicating that the total execution time for this process is approximately 10μs. The response times from when the three threads start requesting to lock the mutex until they successfully lock it are summarized in Table 4.

div.head: D. Analysis of Unlock Delay Response Time
div.p: The method for measuring the actual response time when unlocking a mutex is similar to that used for locking a mutex. In the case of single-threaded operation, the code to unlock the mutex starts at line 245. The theoretical time required for unlocking the mutex is approximately 5.1041 μs. However, under single-threaded conditions, the actual execution time for unlocking the mutex is around 1.372μs. The discrepancy between the actual and theoretical times is on the microsecond level, which falls within an acceptable range.In the test project, the system's running time before and after the thread locks and unlocks the mutex was outputted. This allowed for the calculation of the average actual execution time for three threads to lock and unlock the mutex, as shown in Figure 4. The actual average execution time includes the overhead associated with calling the print function to output information, as well as the time spent by threads entering and exiting various lists and performing context switches.

The following steps were taken in the thread_redlight.c file:Before Locking the Mutex: Before calling the function mutex_take(g_single_light_mutex, WAITING_FOREVER), insert the function call a = rt_tick_get() to obtain the global system tick count. Use a printf statement to output the current tick count when the red light thread begins to request locking the mutex:printf("SysTick Red Light Thread begins to request locking mutex: %d \r\n", a);After Unlocking the Mutex: After the mutex release function mutex_release(g_single_light_mutex), insert the function call d = rt_tick_get() to get the current global system tick count. CONCLUSIONMutexes play a crucial role in ensuring program correctness and resource safety. This paper provides a detailed explanation of the concept of mutexes, their application scenarios, and the process of creating, acquiring, and releasing mutexes in RT-Thread. The execution flow is clearly illustrated through flowcharts. By establishing an experimental platform, we simulated scenarios where threads of equal priority use mutexes to access resources. Through timing analysis and data statistics, we verified the effectiveness and real-time performance of the mutex scheduling mechanism. Theoretical analysis and practical testing were conducted to compare the theoretical response time with the actual response time for locking and unlocking mutexes. We also analyzed the time distribution during which threads hold mutexes. The experimental results indicate that the RT-Thread mutex scheduling mechanism exhibits high comprehensive performance metrics and excellent real-time capabilities. This study provides valuable references for designing new Real-Time Operating Systems (RTOS) and for comparative analysis between different RTOSs.
